tier_reason: The tfjs-backend-wasm README Benchmarks section has first-party MobileNet V2 and Face Detector tables comparing WASM against the same project's plain-JS CPU backend and WebGL (Chrome 79.0, 200-run averages). The harness is public (e2e/benchmarks/local-benchmark), but no CPU models, Emscripten/XNNPACK build flags or SIMD flag settings are stated, so it stays C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README prose: WASM is ~3X-11.5X faster than the plain-JS CPU backend on MobileNet V2 and ~8.2-19.8X faster on Face Detector. Table rows: MobileNet V2 on a ThinkPad X1 Gen6 (Linux) 122.7 ms WASM vs 1489.4 ms plain JS (12.1x, derived from page data, slightly above the prose's 11.5x), WASM + SIMD 34.6 ms and WASM + SIMD + threads 12.4 ms (120x vs plain JS, derived from page data); iPhone XS 140 vs 426.4 ms (3.0x, derived). Face Detector on desktop Linux 12.6 ms vs 249.5 ms (19.8x, derived); iPhone XS 21.4 vs 176.9 ms (8.3x, derived). WebGL is faster than WASM on MobileNet V2 on every device (for example ThinkPad 44.8 ms vs 122.7 ms).
corrections.hardware: iPhone X, iPhone XS, Pixel 4, ThinkPad X1 Gen6 (Linux), desktop Windows, desktop Linux, MacBook Pro 15 2019, plus a Node v14 on MacBook Pro row; CPU models not stated; Chrome 79.0
corrections.workload: MobileNet V2 (3.48M params, ~300M multiply-adds) and Face Detector (0.1M params, ~20M multiply-adds) inference time in ms, averaged over 200 runs, on the tfjs-benchmarks.web.app local-benchmark page (Chrome 79.0) plus one Node v14 row; backends Plain JS (CPU), WebGL, WASM, WASM + SIMD, WASM + SIMD + threads
corrections.caveats: 2020-era first-party numbers on Chrome 79; CPU models and build flags are not stated. WebAssembly SIMD was not on by default in Chrome 79 (it shipped by default in Chrome 91), and the README does not say how the SIMD columns were run. The baseline is the project's own plain-JS CPU backend, a reference backend rather than a tuned JS implementation. The WebGL backend beats WASM on MobileNet V2 on every listed device, and the README's 5.3-7.7X 'slower than WebGL' range does not match all rows (Pixel 4 2.4x, ThinkPad 2.7x, derived). The speed comes from XNNPACK kernels compiled with Emscripten; XNNPACK is a wave-8 incumbent baseline. Threads need cross-origin isolation (COOP/COEP) since Chrome 92, or the backend falls back to SIMD-only. The last commit to tfjs-backend-wasm is 2024-04-12; the monorepo's last commit is 2026-04-06 (a CI chore). The benchmark harness is public in e2e/benchmarks/local-benchmark.

notes: Numbers match the README tables exactly; the prose ranges are slightly off (ThinkPad MobileNet ratio is 12.1x, derived, above the stated 11.5x upper bound), and I added the WebGL-is-faster caveat. Metadata confirmed: Apache-2.0, 19.1k stars, not archived, backend path last commit 2024-04-12 (stale), monorepo 2026-04-06. Category fit: a C++ library (XNNPACK) compiled to wasm and compared with the JS equivalent fits wasm-libraries-and-apps better than assemblyscript-and-wasm-langs; consider a category override.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C. A third-party harness (thevilledev/haya32x64 bench/js.mjs, run as node --expose-gc js.mjs, with xxhash-wasm 1.1.0 and xxhashjs 0.2.2 pinned in bench/package.json) times xxhash-wasm XXH64 against xxhashjs XXH64. docs/benchmarks.md and the raw bench/results JSON state Node.js 24.18.0 / V8 13.6.233.17 and AMD EPYC 9R45 / Arm Neoverse V2 CPUs. The first-party README table (bench/index.js, Benchmark.js) alone would be C, since it gives no CPU model.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Third-party (haya32x64 docs/benchmarks.md, snapshot 2026-08-09, xxhash-wasm 1.1.0 vs xxhashjs 0.2.2, public API, medians of nine 150 ms samples): XXH64 one-shot 4-byte input 39.4 ns vs 1939.3 ns on C8a (AMD EPYC 9R45), about 49x (derived from page data), and 63.9 vs 2691.0 ns on C8g (Neoverse V2), about 42x (derived). 1 MiB bulk 15,973 vs 37 MB/s (about 432x, derived) on C8a and 10,738 vs 28 MB/s (about 384x, derived) on C8g. 8-char strings 59.2 vs 2437.8 ns (about 41x, derived). First-party README (Benchmark.js ops/sec): the prose says the 32-bit hash is up to 90x and the 64-bit up to 350x faster than xxhashjs. The table itself shows 32-bit from 11.2x at 1 byte (5,752,446 vs 513,517 ops/sec) up to 140.7x at 1,000,000 bytes, and 64-bit from 373x at 1 byte (4,438,501 vs 11,896 ops/sec) up to 677.8x at 100,000 bytes. At 100,000,000 bytes 64-bit is 34.56 vs 0.13 ops/sec (265.8x). All README ratios are derived from page data.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Hand-written src/xxhash.wat built with wasm-opt --enable-bulk-memory -O4 (package.json build-wasm script; npm 1.1.0 artifact). Third-party run under Node.js 24.18.0 / V8 13.6.233.17-node.50 via node --expose-gc js.mjs (haya32x64 bench/, calibration plus warmup, then nine 150 ms samples, median). The first-party README table comes from bench/index.js (Benchmark.js, node --max-old-space-size=4096 index.js), with Node 17.3 stated for the Node-crypto table.
corrections.hardware: Third-party: AWS EC2 c8a.2xlarge (AMD EPYC 9R45) and c8g.2xlarge (Arm Neoverse V2), Ubuntu 26.04, timed work pinned to CPU 2. First-party README: an x64 MacBook Pro (CPU model not stated) running Node 17.3; the xxhash-wasm 64-bit column is identical in the xxhashjs and Node-crypto tables, so both appear to come from the same run (inference).
corrections.workload: XXH64/XXH32 hashing via the public JS API. Third-party: byte-array one-shot (4 B, 8 B), 1 MiB bulk, streaming 1 MiB in 64 B-64 KiB chunks, and ASCII strings (8, 32 chars). First-party README: Benchmark.js ops/sec on random ASCII strings from 1 byte to 100,000,000 bytes, plus Node crypto md5/sha1 for comparison.
corrections.caveats: The baseline xxhashjs is a slow pure-JS port that emulates 64-bit math with cuint, not a tuned JS hash. The Node crypto comparison uses cryptographic md5/sha1. There is no native xxHash C baseline. The README prose (up to 90x/350x) understates its own table (up to ~141x/~678x, derived). In the first-party bench/index.js the xxhashjs calls also run .toString(16) on each result while xxhash-wasm returns raw numbers/BigInt, so the baseline does extra work (small at large inputs). Not the fastest wasm xxHash: hash-wasm 4.10.0's README shows XXHash64 at 101.66 MB/s vs xxhash-wasm 1.0.2's 47.58 MB/s at 32 bytes (2.1x, derived), with a tie at 1 MB (15,989 vs 15,929 MB/s). In haya32x64's harness, pure-JS haya32x64 (a different hash) beats xxhash-wasm XXH64 on 4-byte keys (22.9 vs 39.4 ns), and cyrb53 (53-bit) is faster still. The third-party measurer is a competing hash author's new repo (a wave-7 catalog entry), with one instance per host type. WebAssembly instantiation (~1-2 ms) is excluded. Needs BigInt-in-wasm, bulk memory and TextEncoder.encodeInto (Chrome 85+, Safari 15+, Node 15+).

notes: README numbers match the record exactly, but its prose ratios understate the table, and the first-party harness gives xxhashjs extra .toString(16) work. Tier upgraded C to A on the third-party haya32x64 harness, following the libspng-via-wuffs precedent. Metadata confirmed: MIT, 184 stars, 21 forks, not a fork, last commit 2024-11-19 (v1.1.0), stale. Category fit: a hand-written WAT library compared with the JS equivalent fits wasm-libraries-and-apps better than assemblyscript-and-wasm-langs; consider a category override. hash-wasm (already in wave 13 merged) is faster at small inputs.
